title: Feedback loops into evaluation
story:
Production generates evidence about your system continuously, and most teams throw nearly all of it away. Every session in which somebody rephrased the same question three times is a record of a failure. Every answer that was copied and then edited is an expected output somebody wrote for you. Every abandoned conversation is a signal, and none of it is collected because none of it arrives labelled as feedback.

The loop worth building is short: collect the signal, triage it into causes, convert the causes into cases, fix, and keep the case forever as a guard against the same thing returning. The last step is what makes the effort compound rather than repeat. Without it you fix the same class of problem several times and never notice, because nothing was written down that would have caught it coming back.

Explicit feedback is the obvious input and the weakest. A rating is given by people with strong feelings, which is a small and unrepresentative group, and it tells you a direction without a reason. Improve it by making it specific rather than by asking for it more often: a short list of reasons — the answer was wrong, it used the wrong source, it refused when it should not have, it was right but unusable — turns an unusable mood into a triageable category. That list should come from your actual failure modes, and every item on it should map to something a person could act on.

Implicit signals are more plentiful and much noisier. Rephrasing, retrying, abandoning, copying, editing before use, immediately asking a narrower version of the same question — all of these are cheap to record and all of them have innocent explanations. Use them for prioritisation, never for adjudication: they tell you where to look, and a person still has to decide what went wrong when you get there.

Then the trap, which is the reason this lesson is not simply a process. If you optimise the signal, you will get the signal. Ratings improve when a system is agreeable, hedges less and sounds more confident, none of which is the same as being right — so a team steering by satisfaction alone will gradually train an assistant that flatters. That is the same mechanism as optimising any learned proxy, and it arrives here through the product rather than through the training, which is why it is easy to miss.

There is a second trap, sharper and quieter, for any system that feeds its own output back into its inputs. If answers become content, and content is retrieved later, then an error that survives one round becomes a source the next time — and it will be cited, which makes it look better supported each time it recurs. Keep the origin of everything you store, never let generated material enter a corpus without being marked as generated, and treat anything derived from your own output as a claim rather than a source.

Finally, close the loop with the person who reported it, because it costs almost nothing and it is the only thing that keeps reports coming. Somebody who tells you an answer was wrong and hears nothing will not tell you again, and the people most worth hearing from are exactly the ones who stop first. A short note saying what was changed converts a complaint into a continuing relationship, and a system whose users keep reporting problems is in far better shape than one whose users have gone quiet.

problem.name: Turning production evidence into cases
problem.shape: The system produces evidence about its own failures all day and none of it arrives labelled.
tell: feedback exists as a rating with no reason attached
the same class of problem has been fixed more than once
satisfaction is rising and correctness has not been measured
generated answers are stored where retrieval can later find them
problem.move: Collect explicit feedback as a short list of actionable reasons drawn from real failure modes, mine implicit signals for prioritisation only, convert triaged causes into permanent cases, mark the origin of anything generated, and tell the reporter what changed.
problem.invariant: A fix only compounds if it leaves behind a case that fails when the problem returns, otherwise the same class is repaired repeatedly without anyone noticing.
problem.breaks: Steering by satisfaction optimises agreeableness and confidence rather than correctness, and a system that retrieves its own generated output turns a surviving error into a cited source.

cost.time: triage is human work, and the case set has to be maintained as it grows
cost.space: signals and their traces have to be stored and connected to the requests that produced them
cost.beats: waiting for formal evaluation to catch everything, which only tests what you already knew to ask, and acting on raw ratings, which optimises a proxy

problem.practice: Find every session in the last week where the user asked essentially the same thing twice in a row. Read ten of them. Each one is a failure your monitoring did not flag and your case set does not contain, and converting them into cases is an afternoon that permanently improves what you measure.

beats.broke: Production produces evidence of failure continuously and none of it is labelled, so it is discarded and the same classes of problem are repaired repeatedly.
beats.fix: Collect specific reasons rather than ratings, mine implicit signals to decide where to look, and convert triaged causes into permanent cases that guard against recurrence.
beats.cost: Triage is human work, and steering by the signal itself optimises agreeableness rather than correctness.
